title: Safe for Democracy: The United States and World War I
summary: The Progressive presidents projected American power abroad as vigorously as they expanded government at home. Roosevelt engineered Panama's independence to build the Panama Canal and proclaimed the Roosevelt Corollary, claiming an 'international police power' in the Western Hemisphere; Taft favored Dollar Diplomacy; and Wilson's 'moral imperialism' produced more Latin American interventions than any predecessor, including occupations of Haiti and the Dominican Republic and a failed pursuit of Pancho Villa in revolutionary Mexico. Wilson's liberal internationalism held that spreading American trade and values would spread freedom itself.

When Europe went to war in 1914, Wilson proclaimed neutrality, but German submarine warfare—dramatized by the sinking of the Lusitania—and the Zimmermann Telegram pushed the United States into the conflict in April 1917, with Wilson vowing to make the world 'safe for democracy.' His Fourteen Points promised self-determination, free trade, open diplomacy, and a League of Nations. American troops helped turn the tide at Meuse-Argonne in 1918. At home the war built an unprecedented federal state: a draft, the War Industries Board, high taxes and Liberty bonds, and the Committee on Public Information's propaganda. War fervor delivered Prohibition and, after militant campaigning by Alice Paul and patriotic service by millions of women, the Nineteenth Amendment. But the Espionage and Sedition Acts, the jailing of Eugene Debs, and coercive '100 percent Americanism' made the war years the harshest assault on civil liberties in U.S. history.

The war transformed race relations as half a million Black southerners moved north in the Great Migration, only to meet riots in East St. Louis, Chicago, and Tulsa, while the NAACP, Du Bois, and Marcus Garvey's nationalism voiced rising militancy. In 1919, massive strikes and the Red Scare crushed labor and radicalism; abroad, the Versailles Treaty betrayed colonial hopes for self-determination, and the Senate rejected the League. Voters chose Harding's 'normalcy' in 1920.
big_ideas: Progressive-era foreign policy—the Roosevelt Corollary, Dollar Diplomacy, and Wilson's moral imperialism—made the Caribbean and Latin America a sphere of repeated U.S. military and financial intervention.
Submarine warfare, the Lusitania, and the Zimmermann Telegram drew the United States into World War I, which Wilson framed as a crusade to make the world safe for democracy.
War mobilization created a powerful, temporary national state that managed industry, drafted millions, and sold the war through official propaganda.
Wartime idealism helped secure the Eighteenth (Prohibition) and Nineteenth (woman suffrage) Amendments, but the Espionage and Sedition Acts brought the era's most severe repression of dissent.
The Great Migration moved Black southerners to northern industrial cities, sparking both violent white backlash and new forms of Black protest from the NAACP to Garveyism.
In 1919 a global wave of strikes and revolution met fierce reaction; in the U.S. the Red Scare destroyed radical movements and equated patriotism with the status quo.
Wilson's Fourteen Points inspired colonized peoples worldwide, but Versailles's compromises and the Senate's rejection of the League left a legacy of disillusionment and future conflict.

key_terms.def: Wilson's foreign-policy vision that American trade, investment, and intervention abroad would advance both U.S. interests and global political freedom.
Theodore Roosevelt's extension of the Monroe Doctrine asserting a U.S. right to act as an international police power in the Western Hemisphere, used to justify Caribbean interventions.
Waterway completed in 1914 after Roosevelt backed Panama's secession from Colombia; the U.S. gained sovereignty over the Canal Zone, a lasting source of resentment in Latin America.
British liner sunk by a German U-boat with 124 Americans among the dead, outraging U.S. opinion and fueling Wilson's preparedness program.
Intercepted German message proposing that Mexico join a war against the United States in exchange for lost territory; its publication helped push America into World War I.
Wilson's statement of war aims—including self-determination, freedom of the seas, open diplomacy, and a league of nations—that set the agenda for the postwar peace conference.
Law requiring 24 million men to register for the draft, rapidly building the army that fought in France.
Federal agency under Bernard Baruch that directed wartime production, allocated raw materials, and fixed prices, exemplifying the expanded wartime state.
Government propaganda agency led by George Creel that flooded the nation with pamphlets, posters, and films selling the war as a fight for democracy and freedom.
Wartime laws criminalizing interference with the draft and speech critical of the government or war effort; over 2,000 people were prosecuted, including Eugene Debs.
Constitutional amendment barring states from denying the vote on account of sex, won through women's war service and the militant tactics of Alice Paul's National Woman's Party.
Movement of roughly half a million African Americans from the South to northern cities during and after the war, drawn by industrial jobs, schooling, and escape from lynching.
Civil rights organization founded in 1909 by W. E. B. Du Bois and white reformers that fought discrimination through lawsuits and publicized injustice in its journal, The Crisis.
Jamaican-born leader of the Universal Negro Improvement Association whose message of Black pride, self-reliance, and African independence built the era's largest Black mass movement.
Postwar panic over radicalism in which Attorney General Palmer's raids arrested thousands without warrants and deported immigrant radicals, devastating unions and the Socialist Party.

key_terms.term: Treaty of Versailles / League of Nations
key_terms.def: Peace settlement that created Wilson's League and redrew Europe but imposed crushing reparations on Germany and ignored colonial self-determination; the U.S. Senate refused to ratify it.

timeline.event: United States acquires the Panama Canal Zone after backing Panama's break from Colombia
Roosevelt Corollary claims a U.S. police power in the Western Hemisphere
NAACP organized following the Springfield, Illinois, lynching
World War I breaks out in Europe; the Panama Canal opens
German U-boat sinks the Lusitania, killing 124 Americans
Zimmermann Telegram revealed; U.S. declares war on Germany; Espionage Act passed; Russian Revolution begins
Wilson announces the Fourteen Points; Americans fight at Meuse-Argonne; armistice ends the war in November
Versailles Treaty signed; steel strike, race riots, and the Red Scare convulse the U.S.; Eighteenth Amendment ratified
Nineteenth Amendment gives women the vote; Senate rejects the Versailles Treaty; Harding wins on a 'return to normalcy'
Tulsa riot destroys a prosperous Black community, the deadliest racial violence in U.S. history

themes: America in the world: From the Panama Canal to Versailles, the U.S. shifted from hemispheric policeman to global power promoting a Wilsonian model of intervention in freedom's name.
Politics and power: War mobilization vastly expanded federal authority, while the Espionage and Sedition Acts and the Red Scare showed how that power could crush dissent.
American and national identity: Coerced 'Americanization,' anti-German hysteria, and eugenics narrowed national belonging even as suffrage expanded the electorate.
Migration and settlement: The Great Migration remade northern cities and race relations, provoking violence but also new Black political and cultural assertiveness.
Work, exchange, and technology: Wartime labor shortages briefly empowered unions and raised wages, but the 1919 strike wave's defeat reversed labor's gains.
